TITLE: Oxfordshire council reorganisation a mad hokey cokey, says leader - BBC News
DATES: ['2026-11-23T06:17:16.233Z', '2026-11-23T06:17:16.233Z']

BBC HomepageSkip to contentAccessibility HelpYour accountNotificationsHomeNewsSportWeatheriPlayerSoundsBitesizeCBBCCBeebiesFoodMore menuMore menuSearch BBCHomeNewsSportWeatheriPlayerSoundsBitesizeCBBCCBeebiesFoodClose menuBBC NewsMenuHomeUKWorldBusinessCulturePoliticsHealthTechInDepthBBC VerifyClimateMoreScienceFamily & EducationIn PicturesDisabilityNewsbeatEnglandLocal NewsCouncil reorganisation a mad hokey cokey, says leaderImage caption, Tim Bearder has called the reorganisation of local government a "farce"

A government department has admitted mistakes in the latest round of local government reorganisation.

Leaders in Oxfordshire and West Berkshire received a "minded-to" decision letter in October confirming the proposals for the three unitary authorities the government intended to proceed with.

But an "inconsistency" in the description of the Greater Oxford boundary led to confusion over which parishes were to be included.

Liberal Democrat leader of Oxfordshire County Council, Tim Bearder, called it "a mad hokey cokey." A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) said it "remained committed" to the plans.

A three unitary model for Oxfordshire and West Berkshire had been approved in July, starting the process to create a Northern Oxfordshire Council, a Ridgeway Council and a Greater Oxford Authority.

It would mean one council would be responsible for a specific geographical area, rather than the current county, district and city structure.

The process was paused in September when the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government Angela Rayner, announced a review of wider reorganisation plans.

On 29 October, leaders received an update from the government, stating its intention to proceed with the original proposals, but the boundaries contained in the letter showed eight parishes in different unitary areas than first outlined.

Originally, Nuneham Courtenay, Culham, Clifton Hampden, Marsh Baldon, Great Milton, Wheatley, Waterstock, Holton were in the Greater Oxford authority, but they were left out in the October update.

The government has blamed the error on the information received from Oxford City Council, confirming "the written schedule in Oxford City Council's proposal listed 41 parishes, while the accompanying maps showed 49" although it acknowledged "they had previously flagged this inconsistency".

Image caption, Labour leader of Oxford City Council, Susan Brown, welcomed the clarification

The Labour leader of Oxford City Council, Susan Brown, said she welcomed the confirmation of the geography "including clarification of those parishes within Greater Oxford".

Brown said she continued to back the three unitary model and that a Greater Oxford would "give the city the space to build much-needed new homes and create well-paid, secure jobs, while protecting important habitats across our Green Belt".

But Bearder said the process was "a farce".

He represents Wheatley, one of the parishes involved in the confusion and said the decision was not just a "map error" because it affected people's lives.

"Wheatley could well be in an authority run out of Newbury, in the Ridgeway, or it could be in an authority run out of Oxford, but with real concerns about how they would have any democratic say in an administration which is largely a city," he added.

Bearder has now urged people to take part in a three week government consultation, to give feedback on the proposals, arguing one council for Oxfordshire would be the most cost-effective.

According to a letter from MHCLG to local council leaders a "fresh minded-to decision" will now be sent to replace the earlier decision "to ensure that the proposal is described clearly and consistently".

A spokesperson for the department said: "Local government reorganisation will save money for taxpayers in Oxfordshire and across the country and we remain committed to it.

"We'll listen to views before making a final decision, so we encourage the council and others to have their say."

If the proposals are confirmed, elections for the three new councils are expected to take place in May 2028.

The elected councillors will then form shadow authorities to prepare for the new councils.

The new councils are due to take over on 1 April 2029, when Oxfordshire and West Berkshire's seven existing councils will be abolished.
